name: Injection
description: Injection flaws, such as SQL, OS, and LDAP injection occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. The attacker's hostile data can trick the interpreter into executing unintended commands or accessing data without proper authorization.
preventions: Use a safe API that avoids using the interpreter entirely or provides a parameterized interface.
Escape all user-supplied input using the specific escape syntax for that interpreter.
Use LIMIT and other SQL controls within queries.

name: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
description: XSS flaws occur whenever an application takes untrusted data and sends it to a web browser without proper validation or escaping. XSS allows attackers to execute scripts in the victim's browser which can hijack user sessions, deface web sites, or redirect the user to malicious sites.
preventions: Encode all untrusted data based on the HTML context (body, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL).
Use frameworks that automatically escape XSS by design.
Apply Content Security Policy.

name: Broken Authentication and Session Management
description: Application functions related to authentication and session management are often not implemented correctly, allowing attackers to compromise passwords, keys, or session tokens, or to exploit other implementation flaws to assume other users' identities.
preventions: Meet all the requirements in NIST 800-63 for authentication, session management, and passwords.
Avoid custom session ID cookies.
Use multi-factor authentication where possible.

name: Insecure Direct Object References
description: A direct object reference occurs when a developer exposes a reference to an internal implementation object without any access control check or other protection. Attackers can manipulate those references to access unauthorized data.
preventions: Use indirect object references per user or session.
Check access on every use of a direct object reference from an untrusted source.

name: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
description: A CSRF attack forces a logged-on victim's browser to send a forged HTTP request, including the victim's session cookie and any other automatically included authentication information, to a vulnerable web application.
preventions: Include an unpredictable CSRF token in all state-changing requests.
Verify the Origin header.
Use the SameSite cookie attribute.

name: Security Misconfiguration
description: Good security requires having a secure configuration defined and deployed for the application, frameworks, application server, web server, database server, and platform. Secure settings should be defined, implemented, and maintained, as defaults are often insecure.
preventions: Establish a repeatable hardening process for all environments.
Remove all unnecessary features, components, documentation, and samples.
Keep all software up to date.

name: Insecure Cryptographic Storage
description: Many web applications do not properly protect sensitive data, such as credit cards, SSNs, and authentication credentials, with appropriate encryption or hashing. Attackers may steal or modify such weakly protected data to conduct identity theft, fraud, or other crimes.
preventions: Use proven algorithms and key sizes.
Ensure passwords are stored with an adaptive and salted hashing function.
Disable autocomplete on forms collecting sensitive data.

name: Failure to Restrict URL Access
description: Many web applications check URL access rights before rendering protected links and buttons. However, applications need to perform similar access control checks each time these pages are accessed, or attackers will be able to forge URLs to access these hidden pages anyway.
preventions: Implement a consistent authorization mechanism and use it throughout the application.
Deny access by default; require explicit grants for access to any functionality.
Consider using a web application framework that enforces access control automatically.

name: Insufficient Transport Layer Protection
description: Applications frequently fail to authenticate, encrypt, and protect the confidentiality and integrity of sensitive network traffic. When they do, they sometimes support weak algorithms, use expired or invalid certificates, or do not use them correctly.
preventions: Use TLS for all sensitive connections.
Enforce secure cipher suites and disable legacy protocols.
Verify that TLS certificates are valid and from a trusted CA.

name: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards
description: Web applications frequently redirect and forward users to other pages and websites, and use untrusted data to determine the destination pages. Without proper validation, attackers can redirect victims to phishing or malware sites, or use forwards to access unauthorized pages.
preventions: Simply avoid using redirects and forwards.
If used, don't involve user parameters in calculating the destination.
If destination parameters can't be avoided, ensure that the supplied value is valid and authorized for the user.
